source_title_hint: This Secret Release Technique Unlocks Your Feet & Ankles
primary_summary: The video teaches a three‑role foot‑rolling protocol using a lacrosse ball to improve foot mechanics (pronation/supination) by establishing consistent three‑point contacts (heel, big toe, little toe) and releasing the transverse arch, with specific rolling patterns and pressure cues.

classification.usefulness_reason: Provides concrete corrective steps for foot mobility and plantar‑fasciitis management

problem_statements: Inconsistent foot‑to‑ground contact (heel, big toe, little toe) hampers pronation/supination and contributes to plantar fasciitis pain
habits_or_contexts: Rolling the foot mindlessly in random directions often fails to locate tender points
key_visual_points: Three‑point foot contact (heel, big toe, little toe)
Three rolling roles: inside‑heel/big‑toe, transverse‑arch release, outside‑foot contact
Windshield‑wiper motion from 1st metatarsal to 5th toe
advice_mentioned: Maintain even pressure; avoid forcing contacts
Start with foot relaxed, roll in a straight line to ~1 in ahead of heel
warnings_or_limitations: If you cannot feel even pressure on heel and toes, underlying pronation/supination dysfunction may be present; avoid excessive force (keep pressure ≤6/10)

knowledge_units.title: Three‑Role Lacrosse‑Ball Foot Roll
knowledge_units.summary: A structured foot‑rolling protocol using a lacrosse ball to locate and improve heel, big‑toe, and little‑toe contacts and to release the transverse arch.
observable_signs: Inability to feel even pressure on heel and toes
execution_steps: Place a lacrosse ball under the first metatarsal head (or big‑toe ball) while standing with relaxed foot
Roll straight back toward the heel until the ball is ~1 in (2.5 cm) ahead of the heel (Role 1) – feel inside heel and big toe contact
Shift weight to release the transverse arch by rolling from the first metatarsal toward the fifth toe (Role 2) – maintain light pressure
Perform a windshield‑wiper motion from the first metatarsal to under the fifth toe, then roll back to start (Role 3) – locate outside foot contacts without losing inside contacts
cues: Focus on feeling the three‑point contacts
breathing_cues: Inhale as you roll forward, exhale as you roll back
errors_to_avoid: Rolling too quickly or with excessive force
Rolling only in random directions without targeting contacts
when_useful: Clients with plantar fasciitis, limited pronation or supination, or uneven foot pressure
when_not_useful: Acute foot injuries where pressure might aggravate tissue
retest: Re‑assess ability to feel even pressure on heel, big toe, and little toe after 2‑3 sessions
advice: Start with light pressure and increase gradually
